config.title: Infinite Scroll

intro.title: Infinite Scroll
intro.body: In this lesson, you'll build a React component that loads more data automatically as you scroll down the page, creating an infinite scrolling effect. You'll learn how to use the Intersection Observer API to detect when the user reaches the bottom of the content. The main technologies involved are React hooks (useState, useEffect, useRef) and TypeScript for type safety. This pattern is commonly used in social media feeds, product listings, and content-heavy applications to improve user experience.
intro.usecase: Infinite scroll is essential for handling large datasets in modern web applications where loading all content at once would be impractical. You'll find this pattern in social media feeds like Facebook and Twitter, e-commerce product listings on Amazon, and content platforms like YouTube's video suggestions. As a developer, implementing infinite scroll improves user experience by reducing initial load times while providing seamless access to more data as users scroll. This technique is particularly valuable in dashboards displaying analytics, news aggregators, and any application with paginated content where you want to eliminate manual 'Load More' buttons.

objectives: Apply TypeScript interfaces to define the structure of data objects returned from an API.
Use React hooks to initialize and manage state variables for storing fetched data and loading status.
Implement a fetch function to retrieve paginated data from a mock API endpoint.
Execute conditional rendering to display loading indicators when data is being fetched.
Utilize the useEffect hook to trigger data fetching when component mounts or dependencies change.
Construct a scroll event handler to detect when the user reaches the bottom of the page.
Control the infinite scroll behavior by conditionally fetching more data based on scroll position.
Modify state variables to append new data to existing data arrays for continuous display.
Assign unique keys to dynamically rendered list items to maintain React's rendering performance.
Invoke the fetch function with updated page parameters to retrieve subsequent data pages.
Handle edge cases by preventing duplicate API calls while data is already loading.
Return a structured React component that renders an infinitely scrolling list of data items.

steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement with curly braces to bring in both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and useState
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have React and useState available to use in your component.
successCriteria: The code should include an import statement that brings in React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState. This gives you access to React's core functionality and the useState hook for managing state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react' using the correct syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to import both React and useState from the 'react' package using an import statement.

steps.title: Create the main InfiniteScroll component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component called InfiniteScroll that returns JSX.Element. You can use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.hint: Define a component that returns a JSX element, like a div. Remember to include the return type : JSX.Element for TypeScript.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the InfiniteScroll component here
steps.expectedOutcome: A functional component named InfiniteScroll is defined with a return statement that outputs JSX.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the InfiniteScroll component with proper TypeScript typing.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your component is named exactly 'InfiniteScroll' and returns JSX.Element.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've defined a component called InfiniteScroll that returns JSX.Element. Review the example if needed.

steps.title: Initialize items state with useState
steps.instruction: Inside the InfiniteScroll component, use the useState hook to create a state variable called 'items' initialized as an empty array of numbers.
steps.hint: Remember to use TypeScript generics with useState to specify the type as number[].
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing state with an empty array
const [items, setItems] = useState<number[]>([]);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a state variable 'items' that can hold an array of numbers, initialized as empty.
successCriteria: The code should include a useState call with the generic type <number[]> and initialize it with an empty array [].
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the items state with an empty array of numbers. This will store the list of items we'll display and load more of.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you've: 1) Used useState with the correct generic type <number[]> and 2) Initialized it with an empty array [].
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Inside the component, use useState<number[]>([]) to create a state variable called 'items' that starts as an empty array.

steps.title: Initialize loading state with useState
steps.instruction: Inside your InfiniteScroll component, use the useState hook to create a state variable called 'loading' initialized to false. Make sure to specify the type as boolean.
steps.hint: Add a second useState call after your items state. The syntax is similar: const [loading, setLoading] = useState<boolean>(false);
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing a boolean loading state
const [loading, setLoading] = useState<boolean>(false);
steps.expectedOutcome: Your component will have a loading state variable that starts as false, ready to track when data is being fetched.
successCriteria: The type is specified as boolean
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a loading state to track when data is being fetched. This will be essential for showing loading indicators during infinite scroll operations.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check: Did you name the variable 'loading'? Did you set the initial value to false? Did you specify the type as boolean?
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to add a useState call for a boolean loading state. The syntax should look like: const [loading, setLoading] = useState<boolean>(false);

steps.title: Initialize page state with useState
steps.instruction: Initialize a state variable called 'page' to track the current page number. Use useState with a number type and set the initial value to 1.
steps.hint: Add a new useState hook call inside your component, similar to how you created the items and loading states.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing a page state
const [page, setPage] = useState<number>(1);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a page state variable initialized to 1, ready to track pagination for infinite scrolling.
successCriteria: The code should include a useState hook for 'page' with type number and initial value 1.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the page state. This will help track which page of data we're currently loading.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your page state is properly typed as number and initialized to 1.
steps.feedbackWrong: The page state wasn't initialized correctly. Make sure to use useState with a number type and initial value of 1.

steps.title: Define the fetchMoreItems function
steps.instruction: Inside your InfiniteScroll component, define an async function called fetchMoreItems that simulates fetching more items. The function should be defined before the return statement.
steps.hint: Create an async function that uses setTimeout to simulate an API delay. You'll update state inside it in later steps.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have an async function named fetchMoreItems defined inside your component. The function doesn't need to update state yet - that will come in later steps.
successCriteria: The function must be named fetchMoreItems, declared as async, and defined inside the component before the return statement.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the fetchMoreItems function. This async function will handle fetching more items when we implement the infinite scroll logic.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function is named exactly 'fetchMoreItems' and is declared as async. Also ensure it's defined inside the component, not outside.
steps.feedbackWrong: The fetchMoreItems function isn't defined correctly. Remember to create an async function with that exact name inside your component.

steps.title: Implement the loading logic in fetchMoreItems
steps.instruction: Inside the fetchMoreItems function, implement the loading logic: set loading to true, simulate an API delay with setTimeout, then update items and page state.
steps.hint: Use setLoading(true) at the start, then setTimeout to simulate delay. Inside setTimeout, update items with setItems and increment page with setPage.
steps.expectedOutcome: The fetchMoreItems function now sets loading to true, simulates an API delay with setTimeout, updates the items array with new items, increments the page number, and sets loading back to false.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've implemented the loading logic correctly with proper state updates and simulated API delay.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check if you're: 1) setting loading to true at the start, 2) using setTimeout, 3) updating items and page, and 4) setting loading back to false inside the timeout.
steps.feedbackWrong: The fetchMoreItems function needs to implement loading logic with setTimeout. Start by setting loading to true, then use setTimeout to simulate delay, update items and page, and finally set loading back to false.

steps.title: Create the useEffect to load initial data
steps.instruction: Add a useEffect hook that calls fetchMoreItems when the component first renders.
steps.hint: Import useEffect from 'react' and add it inside your component. The dependency array should be empty to run only on mount.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a useEffect hook that triggers fetchMoreItems on initial render.
successCriteria: The code should include: 1) Import useEffect from 'react', 2) useEffect hook inside the component, 3) fetchMoreItems called inside useEffect, 4) Empty dependency array [].
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added useEffect to load initial data when the component mounts.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've: 1) Imported useEffect, 2) Added the useEffect hook inside the component, 3) Called fetchMoreItems inside it, 4) Used an empty dependency array [].
steps.feedbackWrong: The useEffect hook for initial data loading is missing or incorrect. Review the example and try again.

steps.title: Import useEffect from 'react'
steps.instruction: Add the useEffect hook to the existing import statement from 'react'.
steps.hint: Update the import statement to include useEffect alongside React and useState.
steps.expectedOutcome: The import statement should now include useEffect, making it available for use in the component.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported the useEffect hook, which will allow you to handle side effects like loading initial data.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Check that you've added useEffect to the import statement from 'react' with the correct syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement doesn't include useEffect yet. Make sure to add it to the existing import from 'react'.

steps.title: Return the main container div
steps.instruction: In the InfiniteScroll component's return statement, replace the existing div with a div that has the className 'infinite-scroll-container'.
steps.hint: Update the JSX to include the className attribute with the value 'infinite-scroll-container'.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component returns a div element with the class name 'infinite-scroll-container'.
successCriteria: The return statement includes a div with className='infinite-scroll-container'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've set up the main container for the infinite scroll component with the correct class name.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the div has exactly the className 'infinite-scroll-container'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The return statement should contain a div with className='infinite-scroll-container'. Check your JSX syntax.

steps.title: Map and display the items list
steps.instruction: Inside the container div, map through the items state to render each item as a div with text content. Use the items array and the map method to create a list of div elements.
steps.hint:
You can use items.map(item =>
{item}
) to render each item. Remember to add a unique key prop to each div.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will render a list of div elements, each containing text from the items array, inside the main container div.
successCriteria: Use items.map() to iterate over the items array
Return a div element for each item
Include a key prop on each div with a unique value
Display the item text inside each div
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully mapped through the items array to render each item as a div. This is the foundation for displaying the scrollable content.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using items.map() to iterate over the items array and returning a div element for each item with a unique key prop.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Inside the container div, you need to use the map method on the items array to create a div element for each item. Each div should have a key prop and display the item text.

steps.title: Add the loading indicator
steps.instruction: After the items list, conditionally render a loading message when the loading state is true. Add a paragraph element that displays 'Loading more items...' only when loading is true.
steps.hint: Use a ternary operator or logical AND (&&) to conditionally render the loading message based on the loading state variable.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will show a 'Loading more items...' message below the items list when loading is true, and hide it when loading is false.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added conditional rendering for the loading indicator. The message will appear when loading is true and disappear when it's false.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check if you're using the correct state variable (loading) and that the message appears in the right location (after the items list).
steps.feedbackWrong: The loading indicator isn't properly implemented. Make sure to conditionally render a paragraph with the text 'Loading more items...' based on the loading state variable.

steps.title: Create the intersection observer callback
steps.instruction: Define a callback function named handleIntersection that calls fetchMoreItems when triggered.
steps.hint: Create a function that will be called by the Intersection Observer when the observed element enters the viewport.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a handleIntersection function that will be used to trigger data fetching when the user scrolls to the bottom.
successCriteria: The code must include a function named handleIntersection that accepts entries parameter and calls fetchMoreItems when appropriate.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the intersection observer callback that will trigger data fetching when the user scrolls to the bottom of the list.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your handleIntersection function properly calls fetchMoreItems when intersection occurs.
steps.feedbackWrong: The intersection observer callback wasn't defined correctly. You need to create a function named handleIntersection that will trigger data fetching.

steps.title: Add the sentinel element and wire the observer
steps.instruction: Add a sentinel div element at the end of your component's return statement and set up an IntersectionObserver to watch it and call fetchMoreItems when it becomes visible.
steps.hint: Create a div element with a ref, then use useEffect to create an IntersectionObserver that observes that ref element and triggers fetchMoreItems when it intersects.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a sentinel div element at the end and an IntersectionObserver that triggers fetchMoreItems when the sentinel becomes visible.
successCriteria: Add a sentinel div element with a ref
Observer calls fetchMoreItems when intersection occurs
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've successfully added the sentinel element and wired up the IntersectionObserver. This completes the infinite scroll implementation - when users scroll to the bottom, the observer will detect the sentinel and trigger loading more items.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but there are some missing pieces. Make sure you've added both the sentinel div element with a ref AND the IntersectionObserver logic in useEffect that watches it and calls fetchMoreItems when it becomes visible.
steps.feedbackWrong: The implementation is incomplete or incorrect. You need to add a sentinel div element at the end of your component and set up an IntersectionObserver to watch it. When the sentinel becomes visible (intersects), the observer should call fetchMoreItems to load more data.
